samples.text:
The charts shows the main sources of money that a university received in 2005 and 2025.

In 2005 the biggest source of income was government grants, which was 48%. Tuition fees was the second with 27% and research contracts gave 15%. Donations and other sources were very small, only 4% and 6%. So, the government and the students paid for most of the university in that year.

In 2025 the situation was quite different. Tuition fees became the largest source and it increased to 49%, almost the half of all income. On the other hand, government grants decreased very much to 21%. Research contracts had a small rise to 18%. Also donations went up to 5% and other sources went up to 7%, but they were still the smallest. It means that the students paid much more than the government in 2025.

Overall, the university depended on the government in 2005, but in 2025 it get most of its money from the students fees. The other sources did not change a lot during the twenty years.
samples.why: Relevant figures reported accurately · overview present but simple and placed last · repetitive linking and vocabulary (went up, decreased) · several agreement and article errors that do not obscure meaning.

samples.text:
The pie charts illustrate where a university obtained its income from in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, the most significant change was that tuition fees replaced government grants as the university's principal source of funding. The remaining three sources made up a relatively small share of income in both years and rose only slightly.

In 2005, government grants provided almost half of the university's income, at 48%, while tuition fees contributed just over a quarter (27%). Research contracts accounted for 15%, and donations and other sources made up the rest, with 4% and 6% respectively.

By 2025, this situation had been reversed. Tuition fees had risen by 22 percentage points to 49%, making them the dominant source of money. In contrast, the proportion coming from government grants fell sharply to 21%, which was less than half of its previous level. As a result, the university became far more reliant on the money paid by its students. Research contracts increased modestly to 18%, and there were marginal rises in donations and other income, which reached 5% and 7% respectively.
samples.why: Clear overview identifying the key reversal · main features highlighted and compared · logical paragraphing with varied linkers · good collocations (principal source, rose modestly) · frequent error-free sentences.

samples.text:
The two charts compare the proportions of a university's income that came from five different sources in 2005 and 2025.

The most notable development over the twenty years was a reversal in the roles of government funding and student fees: the university shifted from relying chiefly on the state to depending on tuition payments. The three smaller sources, meanwhile, remained broadly stable.

In 2005, government grants were the institution's main source of revenue, supplying 48% of the total, whereas tuition fees contributed 27%. Research contracts made up a further 15%, leaving donations (4%) and miscellaneous income (6%) with only a marginal role.

By 2025, the balance had tipped decisively towards fees. Their share had climbed to 49%, while government grants had shrunk to 21%, a fall of 27 percentage points and considerably less than half their earlier level. In other words, the positions of the two main sources had almost exactly swapped. Research contracts grew modestly to 18%, and donations and other income each edged up by a single point, to 5% and 7% respectively, so these three categories together still generated less than a third of the university's income.
samples.why: Well-selected key features with a skilfully framed overview · accurate, purposeful comparisons (fall of 27 points) · seamless cohesion · precise, natural vocabulary · wide range of structures with no errors.
